threads.body: [General] Clearing the map after `basicRecover` must also clear the eviction marker. If the map had exceeded capacity before recovery, this stale flag makes the next unrelated multiple settle return `EMPTY`, suppressing its valid destination and batch count even though all post-recovery deliveries are tracked. Reset the marker here and add a regression case covering eviction followed by recovery.

replies.body: Addressed in 605f20f041432a099fbbefb8dbb0c84ca9d98af7: Reset the eviction marker when a recover forgets every delivery, and added a regression test covering eviction followed by recovery.

Aggregate `anonymousDestination` independently so a multiple settle across two generated queues still reports `messaging.destination.anonymous=true`, as described by the PR's “when they agree” behavior.

[Testing] This new task is absent from `.github/scripts/instrumentations.sh`, where the other `spring-integration-4.1` task variants are enumerated. Add `spring:spring-integration-4.1:javaagent:testWithRabbitInstrumentationMessagingPreview`; otherwise metadata collection will not run this stable-preview cooperation test.

threads.body:
[General] Clear this per-channel state across automatic connection recovery. RabbitMQ's default autorecovery keeps the logical `Channel` object while replacing its underlying channel, so these old delivery tags remain in the `VirtualField` even though they were requeued and are no longer valid. The first post-recovery multiple settle can therefore aggregate stale destinations and an inflated batch count. Add a recovery lifecycle hook and a regression test; the current `AbstractRabbitMqTest` disables automatic recovery.

This issue also appears in the following locations of the same file:
- line 83
- line 104

replies.body:
Addressed in 2c0603b908980c698ca6808ab64b1e40e9c14429.

Analysis: The comment is correct. Automatic recovery reopens the underlying channel while `AutorecoveringChannel` keeps its identity, so the virtual field survives while the broker's delivery-tag sequence restarts at one. Everything remembered under the old numbering then describes different messages, and a settle after recovery reports their destinations and counts.

The client only exposes recovery through `com.rabbitmq.client.Recoverable`, which the module can't depend on: it supports amqp-client from 2.7.0 and automatic recovery only arrived in 3.3.0, so instrumenting it would mean muzzle-splitting the module for a class the instrumentation is otherwise indifferent to.

Recovery is instead detected from the delivery tags themselves. They increase for the life of a channel, so a delivery whose tag is not above the highest one recorded means the numbering restarted and the channel was recovered. The remembered deliveries are dropped at that point, along with the pending range that a rollback would restore, since the transaction that produced it died with the old channel. The deliveries are dropped rather than marked forgotten because the broker requeued them and will redeliver them under the new numbering, exactly as `basicRecover` does, so they are no longer outstanding under any tag the channel will see. The highest recorded tag is deliberately not reset by `clear`, which serves `basicRecover`: that keeps the same channel and keeps increasing tags, so a reset there would make the next delivery look like a recovery.

The detection is one comparison on a path that already takes the lock, and it can only fire on a tag sequence that a live channel never produces.

There is no regression test. Triggering automatic recovery needs the broker connection to be broken and reestablished, and the shared test base disables automatic recovery for every test in the module; a white-box test isn't possible either, because the virtual field is only resolvable from the agent classloader.

Upsides: A settle after an automatic connection recovery no longer reports attributes belonging to messages from before the recovery, which is the one case where the instrumentation could produce confidently wrong attributes rather than absent ones. The detection works on every supported client version, needs no dependency on the client's recovery types, and costs a single comparison per delivery.

Downsides: Recovery is inferred rather than observed, so the state is only corrected once the first delivery arrives on the recovered channel. A settle issued after recovery but before any redelivery still sees the old state; it can only be a settle of a tag the broker no longer knows, which the broker rejects with a channel error, so the span it produces describes a call that failed anyway.
